chunks: Routing the buck switch node. The question: How should you route the switch node of a buck converter?
The switch node is the point in a buck converter where the two switches connect to the inductor, a coil that smooths current.
It jumps between ground and the input voltage in a few billionths of a second, and it carries the coil's full current.
So its copper must be wide enough for the current, but no larger. Extra copper area leaks noise into nearby wires.
Picture a drum skin being struck over and over. A bigger drum makes more noise.
The switch node is the drum: the bigger its copper area, the more it "shouts" into its surroundings.
But it is also a pipe that must carry enough current, so you can't make it hair thin. Choose the width the current needs and keep the length short.
Left, the SW copper is a short stub from the IC to the inductor, with the feedback trace on the far side.
Right, SW is a pour, has a via, and the FB trace runs right beside it, so the displacement current and the electric field land directly on FB.
Switch node: where the switches and inductor meet, swinging between 0 volts and the input voltage.
Capacitance: two pieces of metal near each other pass fast voltage changes as tiny currents. More facing area means more capacitance.
Ground plane: a solid copper layer under the trace, tied to 0 volts, that catches that leaked current close by.
Feedback trace: the thin wire that tells the chip the output voltage. It is easy to disturb. Via: a plated hole that connects copper on different layers.
Leaked current is i equals C times (how fast the voltage changes). A 12 volts swing in 3 nanoseconds is 4 billion volts per second.
A 2 mm by 8 mm trace over a ground plane has about 3 picofarads, so it leaks about 12 milliamps.
A 10 mm by 10 mm pour has about 19 picofarads and leaks about 76 milliamps, more than six times as much. The short trace is still wide enough for 5 amps.
That is the whole idea: width for the current, minimum area.
"Short and just wide enough.

The switch node carries the inductor current, so I size the width from the IPC chart, about 2 mm for 5 amps, but it swings the input voltage in nanoseconds, so any extra area couples noise, since i equals C dv over dt .
So: direct from the SW pins to the inductor pad, one layer, no vias, no pour, a solid ground plane beneath, nothing sensitive nearby, bootstrap capacitor tight, and a small test pad."
